title: Saving the World's Voices
subtitle: Can a language on the brink of extinction be brought back to life?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken today, around 40 per cent are considered endangered, many with only a handful of elderly speakers. A frequently quoted estimate holds that a language disappears roughly every two weeks, although linguists disagree about how such figures should be calculated, not least because the boundary between a language and a dialect is notoriously hard to draw. What is not in dispute is the trend: fewer than 25 languages, among them Mandarin, Spanish and English, are now the mother tongues of more than half the world's population.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Languages rarely die simply because their last speakers die. More often, they are abandoned. The decisive moment comes when parents stop passing a language on to their children, usually because another language appears to offer better jobs, education or social standing. Sometimes coercion is involved. In nineteenth-century Wales, children caught speaking Welsh in some schools were made to wear a wooden board known as the 'Welsh Not', and in Hawaii a law passed in 1896 required all schooling to be conducted in English. Yet even without punishment, a community can move within three generations from speaking only its ancestral language to barely understanding it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Does this matter? Some economists argue that fewer languages mean cheaper communication and trade; linguists reply that each language is a unique record of how a community has organised its experience. Many Pacific languages, for example, have detailed vocabularies for winds, currents and marine life, and the knowledge embedded in such terms has occasionally helped biologists to identify species previously unknown to science. For the communities concerned, language is bound up with identity, and one study of indigenous communities in British Columbia, Canada, found markedly lower rates of youth suicide where more people knew the ancestral language, though the reasons for the link remain debated.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most celebrated case of revival is Hebrew. For nearly two thousand years it survived as a language of prayer, scholarship and writing, but it was nobody's first language. In the late nineteenth century, Jewish settlers in Palestine set about turning it back into an everyday spoken tongue. Its best-known champion, Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, insisted on speaking only Hebrew at home, so that his son became, it is often said, the first native speaker of the language in modern times. He also compiled a vast dictionary full of newly coined words. Historians now stress that his efforts mattered less than the schools of the new agricultural settlements, where Hebrew became the language of instruction and children carried it home to their parents. Today it has around nine million speakers.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Hebrew's success, however, depended on unusual circumstances. It possessed an enormous written literature; its speakers were building a new society from scratch; and they needed a shared language because they had arrived from dozens of countries speaking Yiddish, Arabic, Russian and much else. Few endangered languages enjoy such advantages. Welsh offers a more typical, if more modest, example. Its decline was slowed by several measures: Welsh-medium schools, the first state-funded one opening in 1947; a Welsh-language television channel, launched in 1982; and legislation requiring public bodies to treat Welsh and English on an equal basis. At the 2021 census about 18 per cent of people in Wales said they could speak Welsh - slightly fewer than in 2011 - but the share of children able to speak it is far higher than in the 1970s, and the government aims for a million speakers by 2050.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In the Pacific, the most influential innovation has been the 'language nest'. In New Zealand in the early 1980s, Māori leaders, alarmed that few children were growing up speaking Māori, established kōhanga reo - literally 'language nests' - in which pre-school children were looked after entirely in Māori, usually by grandparents and other elders who had spoken the language from birth. The idea spread rapidly: within a decade there were hundreds of nests, and the approach was later extended into primary and secondary schools. Activists in Hawaii, where fewer than fifty children could then speak Hawaiian, visited New Zealand and opened their own Pūnana Leo preschools in 1984. Two years later, the state legislature lifted the ban on teaching through Hawaiian, which had technically remained in force for ninety years.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Revival brings its own difficulties. Most of those now speaking Hawaiian, Māori or Welsh learnt it at school rather than at home, and their speech often differs from that of older native speakers, who sometimes complain that it sounds artificial or is shaped by English grammar. Dr Ruth Calloway, a sociolinguist who studies revival movements, believes such tensions are inevitable and not necessarily harmful. 'Every living language changes,' she says. 'The real danger is not that young people speak it differently, but that they stop speaking it once they leave the classroom.' The hardest task, then, is to move the language out of the school and into homes and playgrounds.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: For languages with only a few speakers left, revival on the scale of Hebrew or Māori may be unrealistic, and linguists increasingly concentrate on documentation: recording stories, songs and conversations so that future generations have material to work from. Wampanoag, an indigenous language of the north-eastern United States, had had no speakers for more than a century when members of the community began reconstructing it in the 1990s from written records, including a seventeenth-century translation of the Bible. A few children are again being raised with it. No recording can replace a living community, but it can keep open a door that would otherwise close for good.

groups.stem: Which TWO advantages does the writer say Hebrew had that most endangered languages lack?
options: Its speakers came from many different linguistic backgrounds and needed a common language.
It was still spoken from birth by a group of older people.
A large body of written texts existed in the language.
It was promoted by a national television service.
Public organisations were legally obliged to use it.
groups.evidence: It possessed an enormous written literature; its speakers were building a new society from scratch; and they needed a shared language because they had arrived from dozens of countries
groups.note: B is contradicted (Hebrew 'was nobody's first language'); D and E are measures that helped Welsh, not Hebrew.

groups.stem: Which TWO statements about the language nests are correct, according to the passage?
options: They were first set up by the New Zealand government.
The children were mostly cared for by older people who were native speakers.
They were originally intended for children of primary-school age.
The model was adopted elsewhere in the Pacific.
They led directly to the end of a ban on teaching in Māori.
groups.evidence: usually by grandparents and other elders who had spoken the language from birth
groups.note: B: elders who had spoken Māori from birth; D: Hawaiian activists copied the idea with Pūnana Leo. A is wrong (Māori leaders set them up); C is wrong (they were for pre-school children and only later extended to schools); E confuses the nests with the lifting of the Hawaiian ban in Hawaii.
